nodes.label: 5.0.0: a chart upgrade that changes the configuration restarts the pods
nodes.norm_label: 5.0.0: a chart upgrade that changes the configuration restarts the pods
nodes.rationale: Six operator traps at once: no checksum annotation, probes with no scheme against a TLS listener, no pinnable NodePort, two values files that could not render, and metadata_key_prefix swallowed by the provider config's remain field so the shipped values claimed x-s3ep- while every default install ran on s3ep-.

nodes.label: 5.0.0: wrong or unsupported upload checksums are refused
nodes.norm_label: 5.0.0: wrong or unsupported upload checksums are refused
nodes.rationale: A wrong or malformed checksum answers 400 where it answered 200 on every write path, the xxhash family answers 501, and a multi-object delete without a digest is refused with 400 InvalidRequest.

nodes.label: 5.0.0: clean_http_transfer_chunked and the aws-chunked keys are gone
nodes.norm_label: 5.0.0: clean_http_transfer_chunked and the aws-chunked keys are gone
nodes.rationale: net/http deletes Transfer-Encoding from a server request before dispatch and rejects it on HTTP/2, so the gated branch could never fire on any transport the proxy serves - the decoder goes with the key rather than staying as dead code. aws-chunked framing is always stripped, so no setting can turn a checksum check into accept-and-discard.

nodes.label: 5.0.0: the listing response document changes shape
nodes.norm_label: 5.0.0: the listing response document changes shape
nodes.rationale: ListBucketResult with the S3 xmlns instead of a name derived from the SDK type, Size reports the plaintext length, Owner identifies the requesting client instead of the backend account, and HeadBucket answers 404 for a bucket that does not exist.

nodes.label: Release 5.0.0 - the storage format break
nodes.rationale: Objects written by 3.x or 4.0.x answer 403 InvalidObjectState with no migration; run one version at a time, because an object a 4.0.x replica writes during a mixed rollout is refused afterwards like any other.

nodes.label: The committed graph predates the 5.0.0 removal
nodes.norm_label: the committed graph predates the 5.0.0 removal
nodes.rationale: Built 2026-09-10; a large share of its articles name packages and symbols that no longer exist. Use it for shape, never for facts, and never rebuild it unprompted - that is a manual, user-approved, separately committed step.

nodes.label: Integrity is not configurable and never was a layer
nodes.norm_label: integrity is not configurable and never was a layer
nodes.rationale: It is the storage format itself: there is no encryption.integrity_verification and no off/lax/strict/hybrid mode, and a wrapped data key that does not authenticate answers 403 InvalidObjectState rather than a 5xx, because it is a permanent state of that object and a retrying SDK must not report it as a passing outage.

nodes.label: No backward compatibility; remove unnecessary code
nodes.norm_label: no backward compatibility; remove unnecessary code
nodes.rationale: The stored-object format may change without a migration path; the precondition - that no deployment holds data which must stay readable - was confirmed with the repository owner rather than assumed (ADR 0017).

nodes.label: Commits drive the release
nodes.rationale: feat produces a minor; fix, perf, refactor and revert a patch; docs, style, chore, test, build and ci produce no release.

nodes.label: Checklist: adding a chart value
nodes.rationale: Revert the template change and confirm the test goes red - an assertion that passes against both the fixed and the broken chart is not a test.

nodes.label: The committed graphify knowledge graph
nodes.rationale: Fastest way to see how the pieces hang together, but it lags the code: treat a hit as a pointer and verify it in the tree before citing it. Rebuilding is a manual step committed as its own change.

nodes.label: There is no DEK provider extension point
nodes.norm_label: there is no dek provider extension point
nodes.rationale: The data layer is the segment chain; changing it is a storage format change (ADR 0003, ADR 0017).

nodes.label: A whole-object GET is tail-first
nodes.rationale: bytes=-65604 first, then the remainder under If-Match on the first answer's entity tag; the served length and x-amz-checksum-crc32c come from the trailer, not from what the backend says about itself (ADR 0003 D14).

nodes.label: Envelope encryption: DEK per object, KEK wraps DEKs only (D1, D2)
nodes.norm_label: envelope encryption: dek per object, kek wraps deks only (d1, d2)

nodes.label: Stored-length well-formedness guard, never a fabricated plaintext size (D12a)
nodes.norm_label: stored-length well-formedness guard, never a fabricated plaintext size (d12a)

nodes.label: There is no migration; the operator uploads from source (D3, D5)
nodes.norm_label: there is no migration; the operator uploads from source (d3, d5)
nodes.rationale: No re-encryption job, no in-place converter, no dual-format reader and no procedure for extracting plaintext from a bucket the new release cannot read. A migration tool was rejected because it is the read-only path in a different binary, holding plaintext outside the proxy while it runs.

nodes.label: An object the release did not write is refused, never guessed at (D4)
nodes.norm_label: an object the release did not write is refused, never guessed at (d4)
nodes.rationale: 403 InvalidObjectState on GET, HEAD and ranged GET, with no opt-out setting. 'Detect the format and read whatever fits' was rejected outright: the format would be decided by metadata a hostile backend can edit, so the backend picks the reader.

nodes.label: The upgrade is rehearsed once on a running stack (D6)
nodes.norm_label: the upgrade is rehearsed once on a running stack (d6)
nodes.rationale: Run 2026-09-11 against a 4.0.3 proxy across all three write paths under deliberately the same KEK, so the outcome is about the format and nothing else: the stale configuration stopped the new build first, then all three objects answered 403 InvalidObjectState, and a fresh upload matched by SHA-256. It is the only step that proves the release notes describe what actually happens.

nodes.label: The line before a major is end-of-life at the major (D11)
nodes.norm_label: the line before a major is end-of-life at the major (d11)
nodes.rationale: No security patches, no fixes, no backports: one supported line, the newest. No deployment is known on the old lines and the old format is one the product no longer describes as fit for an untrusted backend, so keeping it alive would be work spent on a state the product has left.

nodes.label: A major's notes are assembled from breaking footers (D10)
nodes.norm_label: a major's notes are assembled from breaking footers (d10)
nodes.rationale: Amended 2026-09-14 after rendering the 5.0.0 notes: a keyword matches case-insensitively with an optional colon, so a body opening 'Breaking Change Guard and Version Dry Run had become...' was injected headless and mid-sentence, and markers on non-releasing commit types announced that the test suites were failing. A note now counts only as a real footer with its colon on a commit type that releases something. An x.0.0 opens with the compatibility statement as a banner, not wherever the sort puts it.

nodes.label: On read the exit provider still decrypts, per object (D4, D5)
nodes.norm_label: on read the exit provider still decrypts, per object (d4, d5)
nodes.rationale: The object's own key fingerprint selects the provider that wrapped its data key, so that provider must stay configured - removing it is 'do not delete the key' said in configuration. A whole-object read stays one forward pass and HEAD reads no trailer, so both state the length the stored size implies and neither carries x-amz-checksum-crc32c. Under exit a foreign object is a normal thing to find and is served verbatim; an object that IS ours and cannot be opened is still refused.

nodes.label: The Second Backend Request of a Whole-Object Read Costs About 300 Microseconds
nodes.norm_label: the second backend request of a whole-object read costs about 300 microseconds

nodes.label: Envelope encryption, one data key per object
nodes.norm_label: envelope encryption, one data key per object
nodes.rationale: A random AES-256 DEK per object wrapped under the KEK with an authenticated wrap that fails closed; compromising one DEK compromises one object.

nodes.label: Foreign objects are refused, not served
nodes.norm_label: foreign objects are refused, not served
nodes.rationale: No s3ep-* metadata, an unreadable format or key material that fails its tag answers 403 InvalidObjectState; there is no pass-through opt-out.

nodes.label: No server-side copy (422 NotSupportedWithEncryption)
nodes.rationale: A copy runs inside the backend, where the proxy cannot decrypt and re-encrypt.

nodes.label: SSE-C refused with 501 NotImplemented
nodes.rationale: No read path carries the customer key, so such an object could never be read back.

nodes.label: s3ep-gcm-seg-v2 stored format
nodes.rationale: One format only, no second cipher and no format switch, so there is one answer on every read path instead of a matrix of them.

nodes.label: LRU DEK cache, 1024 entries
nodes.rationale: Keyed by fingerprint, object key and a hash of the wrapped DEK; it is part of what an attacker who takes the process gets.

nodes.label: Where an integrity failure surfaces: before or after the response begins
nodes.norm_label: where an integrity failure surfaces: before or after the response begins
nodes.rationale: Once a status line is out the only signal is aborting the body, so a prefix of authentic plaintext is released and a client that retries on ErrUnexpectedEOF accepts a truncated object; the tail-first read narrowed this to faults inside a segment.

nodes.label: H-2 Per-chunk signatures are never verified
nodes.norm_label: h-2 per-chunk signatures are never verified
nodes.rationale: Accepted: chunk signatures protect the client leg and the adversary is on the other leg. The seed signature never covered the body anyway and UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD is already accepted; TLS on the client leg is the mitigation.

nodes.label: H-3 Rollback and object substitution are not prevented
nodes.norm_label: h-3 rollback and object substitution are not prevented
nodes.rationale: Structural: an older version of the same key is a correctly sealed object the proxy itself wrote. Substitution across keys is closed by the per-segment binding; substitution across time is not, and the only defence is the client's own consistency checks plus backend versioning and object lock.

nodes.label: Handlers that refuse rather than pretend
nodes.norm_label: handlers that refuse rather than pretend
nodes.rationale: An operation that answers 200 for work it did not do is worse than one that refuses: ?attributes returned object bytes, UploadPartCopy silently stored a 0-byte part, the legal-hold handler always set the hold ON, and an unrouted bucket sub-resource fell through so DELETE /bucket?encryption deleted the bucket.

nodes.label: A configuration change rolls the pods
nodes.norm_label: a configuration change rolls the pods
nodes.rationale: Without a checksum annotation helm upgrade reported success while old pods kept the old key encrypting - the deployment tooling handing the operator a false statement about the security of their data. An externally managed ConfigMap or Secret still needs a manual rollout restart, because the chart cannot hash what it does not render.

nodes.label: KEK/DEK key hierarchy, two layers and no third
nodes.norm_label: kek/dek key hierarchy, two layers and no third
nodes.rationale: Integrity is not a value derived alongside the data and stored next to it; it is the tag on every segment, produced by the same operation that encrypts it.

nodes.label: The signature does not cover the body
nodes.norm_label: the signature does not cover the body
nodes.rationale: A missing X-Amz-Content-Sha256 becomes UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD rather than a rejection, and the pre-signed form defaults to it, so the signature authenticates the request line and headers only.

nodes.label: pprof runs on its own loopback listener, non-loopback refuses the start
nodes.norm_label: pprof runs on its own loopback listener, non-loopback refuses the start
nodes.rationale: /debug/pprof/heap on a process holding KEK material, DEKs and plaintext buffers is a key disclosure primitive; the log line that told the operator to restrict access was a control existing only in documentation.

nodes.label: An attacker who takes the proxy gets everything
nodes.norm_label: an attacker who takes the proxy gets everything
nodes.rationale: KEK, DEK cache, in-flight plaintext, the backend credential and every plaintext client secret. There is no HSM path and no separate signing identity; the proxy is the trust anchor.

nodes.label: The sealed trailer authenticates length and CRC32C
nodes.norm_label: the sealed trailer authenticates length and crc32c
nodes.rationale: Carries an index no segment can reach plus the plaintext length and a CRC32C over it, so truncation and extension fail; the CRC32C stays sealed inside the trailer rather than in metadata to deny a hostile backend a confirmation oracle.

nodes.label: Segment seal bound to format id, object key and index
nodes.norm_label: segment seal bound to format id, object key and index
nodes.rationale: The additional data of segment i is s3ep-gcm-seg-v2 || object key || i, so a segment cannot be moved to another position, to another object, duplicated or dropped without the read failing.

nodes.label: The three rules that decide every question
nodes.norm_label: the three rules that decide every question
nodes.rationale: Integrity means the proxy verifies; a control that exists only in configuration is worse than none; the stored format may change without a migration path.

nodes.label: Client upload checksums are the one control on the client leg
nodes.norm_label: client upload checksums are the one control on the client leg
nodes.rationale: A byte corrupted before encryption is sealed faithfully and every later integrity mechanism confirms the corruption; only the checksum the client already computed can catch that. The verdict precedes the commit: the final payload byte is held back until it is in.

nodes.rationale: Generated by semantic-release from the commit headers that reach main.

nodes.norm_label: adr 0017 stored data compatibility is not owed

nodes.norm_label: rendering a shipped values file is not the check
nodes.rationale: helm unittest builds values with set: and never loads those files, so a green Helm job says templates produce manifests and nothing about whether a manifest describes a pod that starts. Extract the rendered ConfigMap and start the binary against it - configuration is validated before the licence is read, so it needs no token.

nodes.norm_label: adr 0013 d1: a configuration key exists only if code reads it and that read changes behaviour

nodes.label: Backward-compatibility code is deleted, not carried (D9)
nodes.norm_label: backward-compatibility code is deleted, not carried (d9)
nodes.rationale: The whole-object aes-gcm path, the streaming aes-ctr path, the separate integrity layer and the unprefixed-metadata fallbacks are gone; s3ep-aes-iv and s3ep-hmac are neither written nor read. The cost, accepted: if the precondition ever fails, the read-only fallback starts from a released version rather than from dormant code - a reader kept in the tree is a reader whose defects ship in every deployment.

nodes.label: No compatibility is owed for data at rest (D1, D2)
nodes.norm_label: no compatibility is owed for data at rest (d1, d2)
nodes.rationale: The choice was never break-or-not, it was break or ship two readers. The precondition - no known deployment holds data that must survive - is confirmed with the owner per breaking release. The fallback is a read-only path for the previous format, a design rather than a built feature.

nodes.label: There is no downgrade, and old ciphertext does not disappear
nodes.norm_label: there is no downgrade, and old ciphertext does not disappear
nodes.rationale: Once objects are written in the new format, returning to the previous release makes them unreadable in the other direction, and nothing prevents or warns about that move. On a versioned bucket the old versions remain unreadable and pay storage; under a retention lock they cannot be removed at all.

nodes.label: Everything that forces operator action ships in one major (D10)
nodes.norm_label: everything that forces operator action ships in one major (d10)
nodes.rationale: Every additional format break costs another full re-upload of every object, which is what makes bundling non-negotiable. The price is that the defects motivating it - unverified ranged reads, a tamper no setting refuses, keystream re-use on a re-uploaded part - stay shipped until the major lands.

nodes.label: The transform is applied at exactly one boundary (D8)
nodes.norm_label: the transform is applied at exactly one boundary (d8)
nodes.rationale: Above the proxy/backend boundary every key is the client's, so signatures, associated data, logs and error documents are correct by construction; below it every key is the stored one and no handler ever sees a stored key. Transforming at each call site would mean every key-bearing call is one more chance to forget one, and forgetting one is silent. Keeping it strictly BELOW the crypto layer is what makes the feature a rename rather than a re-encryption.

nodes.label: Checksums are verified, never forwarded and never stored
nodes.norm_label: checksums are verified, never forwarded and never stored
nodes.rationale: The value describes plaintext while the uploaded body is ciphertext, and a plaintext checksum beside the ciphertext would hand a hostile backend a confirmation oracle for small or low-entropy objects.

nodes.label: A control that exists only in configuration is worse than no control
nodes.norm_label: a control that exists only in configuration is worse than no control
nodes.rationale: Because it gets relied upon: a dropped preference is a missing feature, a dropped guard is a false assurance, and the second is worse than never offering it.

nodes.rationale: Coverage is reported per pull request as a signal, not a gate - no threshold fails the build, so a drop needs a reason rather than a waiver.

nodes.rationale: TestEveryBackendCallCarriesTheOwnerGuard parses the handler sources; the field must be set inside the input literal - an assignment after it works at runtime but fails the test deliberately, so a call site reads as one thing.

nodes.rationale: Race detector is its own job rather than a flag because it costs 2-20x runtime and 5-10x memory; conformance runs one runner per backend with fail-fast off, because when one backend disagrees what the others did is the finding.

nodes.norm_label: paid conformance runs on a schedule, never on a pull request
nodes.rationale: Billed backends charge every written byte for ninety days and a fork's pull request must never reach the credentials (ADR 0027).

nodes.rationale: Adding a job has a second step outside the repo: merge the workflow first, then add the context, or every pull request waits on a check that never reports. Semantic Release is deliberately off the list because branch protection counts a skipped check as passing.

nodes.label: AES-SIV-CMAC (RFC 5297) under a 512-bit name key, AD binds s3ep-name-v1 (D4)
nodes.norm_label: aes-siv-cmac (rfc 5297) under a 512-bit name key, ad binds s3ep-name-v1 (d4)
nodes.rationale: The associated data binds the version label, the segment's depth and the CIPHERTEXT of its parent chain, so a subtree the backend moves or duplicates fails to decrypt in its new place and each segment stays verifiable without decrypting its ancestors - which is what a listing needs. The bucket is deliberately NOT in the AD, mirroring the storage format, so a ciphertext bucket can be replicated wholesale. Encoded base64url without padding: no '/', no URL escaping, case-sensitive like S3 keys.

nodes.label: Only directory segments are encrypted; the leaf stays clear (D2)
nodes.norm_label: only directory segments are encrypted; the leaf stays clear (d2)
nodes.rationale: Encrypting the whole key kills prefix listing: clients list with prefixes that end INSIDE a leaf name - the content-addressed uploader lists by single-letter blob prefixes - and an encrypted leaf has no usable prefix, so such a client cannot open its repository at all. The cost is that leaf names stay readable, which in some layouts is more than it sounds like.

nodes.label: encryption.filename_encryption, off by default (D1)
nodes.rationale: Decided and NOT implemented; it does not ship in 5.0.0. When off, no transform is installed at all - that is the price of it being opt-in and also the reason it can ship. Enabling it on an existing bucket is a rename pass, never a re-encryption.

nodes.label: A transformed key over the 1024-byte S3 limit is refused by the proxy (D13)
nodes.norm_label: a transformed key over the 1024-byte s3 limit is refused by the proxy (d13)
nodes.rationale: With a distinct documented error instead of being sent to the backend to fail obscurely. Each directory segment grows by a 16-byte tag and then by 4/3 base64 expansion - 63 characters become 106 - so the effective client-key limit is lower and depends on depth.

nodes.label: Listing under name encryption: prefix split, backend order, undecryptable keys dropped (D9-D12)
nodes.norm_label: listing under name encryption: prefix split, backend order, undecryptable keys dropped (d9-d12)
nodes.rationale: A prefix ending inside a directory segment cannot be translated and returns an empty listing, documented rather than papered over. Only '/' and the empty delimiter are accepted; any other is refused with InvalidArgument rather than answered wrongly. Keys that do not decrypt are dropped, logged and counted - failing the whole listing would hand the backend a one-object denial of service, and because the transform is authenticated, dropped means exactly 'not written by this proxy'. Backend order is returned unsorted: sorting one page is a lie that looks like an order, sorting globally means buffering the whole listing.

nodes.label: The names subcommand: wrap, map, unmap (D16)
nodes.norm_label: the names subcommand: wrap, map, unmap (d16)
nodes.rationale: names wrap generates a name key, wraps it under the configured active KEK and prints the configuration block; names map and names unmap apply the transform in each direction, for a migration or a debugging session.

Names are different - an avoidable disclosure. Bucket configuration documents carrying key prefixes stay untransformed and are recorded as DELIBERATELY untransformed so a later implementation does not inherit a wrong answer in silence.

nodes.norm_label: the e2e harness has two halves
nodes.rationale: stored.go and atrest.go take client and bucket as parameters and know nothing about where a stack lives, which is what lets Velero in a kind cluster share them; putting a demo-stack lookup into the shared half breaks Velero at runtime, not at compile time.

nodes.label: One tool, one suite, one job - never bundled
nodes.norm_label: one tool, one suite, one job - never bundled
nodes.rationale: A red gate names the client in the job name; one client's trouble cannot withhold the other's verdict; a required check is per job, so bundling makes it impossible to require one client and not another. Job names read E2E <tool> (<backend>) because the procedure is what groups them and a verdict is about the backend.

nodes.label: Checklist: adding a KEK provider
nodes.rationale: Fingerprint() must identify the key without revealing anything about it and must be stable: it is what a stored object names, so a provider that changes its fingerprint stops reading its own objects.

nodes.label: Checklist: adding an end-to-end client suite
nodes.norm_label: checklist: adding an end-to-end client suite
nodes.rationale: Its own job and its own Make targets, never added to an existing client's, so a red gate names the tool and one tool's trouble cannot withhold another's verdict. CI runs the same up/down scripts a workstation does, which keeps the two from drifting.

nodes.label: A ranged read plans without a key
nodes.norm_label: a ranged read plans without a key
nodes.rationale: PlanRange maps the plaintext range onto stored bytes so the backend request is issued before anything is unwrapped; a suffix or open-ended range costs a HEAD first because both are relative to the end.

nodes.norm_label: s3_backends (a list of exactly one entry)

nodes.label: License validation is part of configuration validation (D1)
nodes.norm_label: license validation is part of configuration validation (d1)
nodes.rationale: A bad or missing license is a startup failure, not a degradation: there is no grace-period mode. The gate reads only the ACTIVE provider, which is what lets a lapsed license stop new encryption without stopping reads under exit.

nodes.label: A removed configuration key is removed - no alias, no shim (D7)
nodes.norm_label: a removed configuration key is removed - no alias, no shim (d7)
nodes.rationale: encryption.integrity_verification with its off/lax/strict/hybrid modes, optimizations.streaming_threshold, streaming_buffer_size, enable_adaptive_buffering, the backend use_tls, the never-read encryption.algorithm and key_rotation_days and the legacy top-level backend block all went at once. A deprecation window was rejected: a declared key that does nothing is the dead-control failure.

nodes.label: One 64-byte name key per deployment, wrapped by the active KEK (D6, D7, D15)
nodes.norm_label: one 64-byte name key per deployment, wrapped by the active kek (d6, d7, d15)
nodes.rationale: Not derived from the KEK: deriving would rename every object on every KEK rotation, turning a cheap metadata-only operation into a full bucket rewrite, and a KMS-backed provider hands out a handle rather than bytes so there is nothing to derive from. Unwrapped once at startup, never on the request path. With enabled:true the proxy refuses to start on a missing wrapped_key, an unknown kek_fingerprint, a failed unwrap, or an active exit provider - there is no fall back to cleartext names.

nodes.label: The exit provider requires no licence (D2)
nodes.norm_label: the exit provider requires no licence (d2)
nodes.rationale: Getting data out is exactly the situation in which a licence cannot be assumed valid, so making it a condition would defeat the purpose. The gate examines the active provider only, so exit starts without one while an encrypting provider stays registered.

nodes.label: The exit provider (D1)
nodes.rationale: The supported way to stop using the product without losing access to what it already encrypted. A product that encrypts data at rest owes its operator a way out, or the encryption is not a feature but a hostage. It is not a testing aid, not a development mode and not a way to run the proxy as a plain pass-through in production.

nodes.label: On write the exit provider stores what the client sent (D3)
nodes.norm_label: on write the exit provider stores what the client sent (d3)
nodes.rationale: No data key, no wrap, no proxy metadata, on all three write paths. The partial pass-through this replaced - plaintext for small objects, ciphertext for large ones with the key wrapped by a no-op encryptor and stored beside the object - is worse than either alternative, because a bucket then looks protected while the key sits next to it.

nodes.label: type: "none" is refused by name (D9)
nodes.rationale: With a message naming exit and saying to keep the provider holding the old key configured alongside it. No silent alias and no deprecation period. The name was the smallest problem and the clearest signal: none described a provider that did something, and the one mode meant to be the way out was the mode in which the old data became unreadable.

nodes.label: An active exit provider says so at every start (D10)
nodes.norm_label: an active exit provider says so at every start (d10)
nodes.rationale: It logs that new objects are stored unencrypted and that previously encrypted ones stay readable while their provider is configured. A warning, not an error: the operator asked for this. Nothing enforces keeping the old provider, because nothing can distinguish removal from a deliberate decommissioning.

nodes.label: Under the Exit Provider There Is No Session at All
nodes.norm_label: under the exit provider there is no session at all

nodes.label: The Exit Provider's Branch on Every Read and Write Path
nodes.norm_label: the exit provider's branch on every read and write path

nodes.label: aes KEK provider
nodes.rationale: aes_key is base64 of exactly 32 random bytes; the key is never used directly - wrapping key and published fingerprint are HKDF-SHA256 derivations under separate labels, so the fingerprint reveals nothing about the key.

nodes.label: exit provider - leaving is a supported mode
nodes.norm_label: exit provider - leaving is a supported mode
nodes.rationale: Needs no licence on purpose: getting data out must never depend on a licence being valid. Stores what the client sends, still decrypts what aes wrote, and decides per object.

nodes.label: Key rotation without re-encryption
nodes.rationale: Every object names the key that wrapped it, so rotation is a configuration change; dropping a retired key makes every object written under it permanently unreadable.

nodes.label: The licence is a startup gate
nodes.norm_label: the licence is a startup gate
nodes.rationale: With an active aes provider and no valid licence the proxy refuses to start and names what is missing; the exit provider is exempt so a lapsed licence never blocks reading your own data (ADR 0016).

nodes.label: Ranged reads fetch only the covered segments
nodes.norm_label: ranged reads fetch only the covered segments
nodes.rationale: Byte-range clients such as kopia, and therefore Velero volume backups, work at full speed.

nodes.label: Proven clients: Velero, rclone, s3cmd
nodes.rationale: Compatibility is argued from S3 semantics rather than from one observed client (ADR 0006); three clients are additionally proven each release by an e2e suite driving a pinned real binary.

nodes.label: What the exit provider means for the threat model
nodes.norm_label: what the exit provider means for the threat model
nodes.rationale: Selecting exit moves plaintext below the trust boundary on purpose - the operator's declared intent, not a defect. Encrypted objects are still authenticated, the namespace is still refused to clients, and the switch back to aes is a one-way door for objects written behind it.

nodes.label: H-4 Velero kopia repositories default to a published password
nodes.norm_label: h-4 velero kopia repositories default to a published password
nodes.rationale: With static-passw0rd, kopia's AES-GCM and content HMACs are forgeable by anyone who can read the bucket because the salt sits in the same bucket; the proxy is then the only protection. Must be set before the first backup - changing it later does not re-key the repository.

nodes.label: KEK rotation by fingerprint
nodes.rationale: Fingerprints are derived, not configured, so they cannot drift; the KeyEncryptor interface has no RotateKEK call because rotation is the configuration procedure, not an API call.

nodes.label: Licence expiry stops the proxy through the drain path
nodes.norm_label: licence expiry stops the proxy through the drain path
nodes.rationale: Reading the data back needs no licence: point the alias at an exit provider with the aes provider listed beside it. Not knowing that is what makes people copy ciphertext out of the bucket and hunt for the key by hand.

nodes.rationale: Its consequence is documented as a security-relevant availability property: an expired license stops all new encryption and stops reads until the operator acts. Doing neither remedy leaves every object in the bucket unreadable.

nodes.norm_label: a listing reports the stored size verbatim under exit (d8)
nodes.rationale: Inverting the size arithmetic would under-report some plain objects whose size coincides with an acceptable stored size. Over-reporting costs a client a re-transfer; under-reporting can make a synchronising client believe the remote copy is short and write over it. The safe direction to be wrong in is the one that costs bandwidth.

nodes.norm_label: a ranged read costs one extra head under exit
nodes.rationale: The stored window for an encrypted object is not the plaintext range, so the proxy must know which kind of object it is before asking for a byte range. Exit is a migration state rather than a steady one, which is what makes the extra request acceptable; the cost is reasoned, not measured.

nodes.norm_label: every design decision is recorded as an adr
nodes.rationale: Written in the session the decision is taken, and carrying no references into the code so it stays true when the tree moves; the product's own vocabulary is not a code reference and must be exact.

nodes.label: Documentation has five homes, a statement goes to exactly one
nodes.norm_label: documentation has five homes, a statement goes to exactly one
nodes.rationale: ADR for decisions, docs/developer/ for how a subsystem works, docs/operations/ for the operator, SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE.md for the threat model, a ticket for outstanding work. The difference between developer and operations pages is the reader, not the depth (ADR 0035).

nodes.norm_label: a test asserts the target behaviour, never today's
nodes.rationale: Got wrong on 2026-09-13: every open defect was recorded as an expected refusal, so both client suites were green and the release gate reported a product that could neither upload nor download a single-request object as ready to merge. Committing a red test is allowed and wanted; skipping and pinning are the same mistake in different clothes (ADR 0031, ADR 0019).

nodes.label: A ticket is a work list and nothing else
nodes.norm_label: a ticket is a work list and nothing else
nodes.rationale: The extraction is the close, not the move: an archived file is history and never a source of a current rule, so a rule found there is the same process defect as a rule found in a live ticket (ADR 0022).

nodes.norm_label: documentation updated in the same change, in the right place

nodes.label: The integration and e2e suites are the product's behaviour
nodes.norm_label: the integration and e2e suites are the product's behaviour
nodes.rationale: They are never skipped, disabled or deleted to make a change land; if one fails, the change is not finished (ADR 0019).

nodes.label: The license expiry is discovered by a build, not by an environment (D8, D9, D10)
nodes.norm_label: the license expiry is discovered by a build, not by an environment (d8, d9, d10)
nodes.rationale: Decided and NOT implemented (verified 2026-09-12: no job checks the claim, make check-license does not exist). It would fail - not warn - 14 days before expiry, as the first step of every job consuming the token plus a daily schedule, reading the payload without verifying the signature. A warning annotation was rejected: the proxy's own 30-day startup warning already existed and was ignored.

nodes.label: Breaking changes collect on one long-lived branch (D7, D8)
nodes.norm_label: breaking changes collect on one long-lived branch (d7, d8)
nodes.rationale: Each unit of work is its own squash-merged PR into that branch so a single unit can be reverted alone; nothing releases from it, and the e2e suite gates every rebase onto main. Meanwhile main keeps shipping patches and minors on the current major line.

nodes.label: The release:major label declares a major (D3, D4)
nodes.norm_label: the release:major label declares a major (d3, d4)
nodes.rationale: Applying it is the deliberate act and no other signal declares a major. The label name is a bare convention with no meaning to any tool but the guard that reads it, so renaming or misspelling it silently disarms the guard.

nodes.label: The integration suite runs over plain HTTP and TLS (D5)
nodes.norm_label: the integration suite runs over plain http and tls (d5)
nodes.rationale: The AWS SDK emits STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER framing only over HTTPS. Measured: a TLS run hits the buffered chunked path 718 times, a plain-HTTP run zero. One transport is not a cheaper sample of the other, it is a different code path - a defect that stored chunk framing as object payload lived in it. Runtime is answered with parallel jobs, never a dropped run.

nodes.label: Every e2e suite gates the release (D9)
nodes.norm_label: every e2e suite gates the release (d9)
nodes.rationale: e2e-velero, e2e-rclone and e2e-s3cmd are on semantic-release's needs list with their job names on the required-check list. Taking one off the gate is a deliberate, temporary, recorded act, never a way past a failure. One tool, one job: a red gate has to name the client, and one client's trouble must not withhold another's verdict.

nodes.label: A test pinning soon-to-be-replaced behaviour carries an in-source marker (D16)
nodes.norm_label: a test pinning soon-to-be-replaced behaviour carries an in-source marker (d16)
nodes.rationale: The marker names the change so the churn is localised and greppable. Clarified 2026-09-13 against ADR 0031 D4: this sanctions a test asserting behaviour that is CORRECT TODAY and that a decided change will replace, never licence to assert an answer the product is not supposed to give.

nodes.label: One bring-up script on a workstation and in CI (D7)
nodes.norm_label: one bring-up script on a workstation and in ci (d7)
nodes.rationale: CI carries no bespoke bring-up, so a workstation and a runner cannot drift apart - a CI-tuned bring-up produces 'green in CI, red on my machine', which is unfixable by the person who has to fix it. Re-testing reloads a freshly built image into the existing cluster rather than recreating it.

nodes.label: Environment version pins move as one reviewed group (D8)
nodes.norm_label: environment version pins move as one reviewed group (d8)
nodes.rationale: Automatic merging stays off against a repository default of automerge: a backup client and the chart that installs it are versioned separately, and upgrading one without the other produces an environment that is not the supported one. A pin nothing watches is an unmanaged network dependency of every run.

nodes.label: Test doubles live in test files and exist once (D15)
nodes.norm_label: test doubles live in test files and exist once (d15)
nodes.rationale: Asserted against the interface they stand in for so a change to that interface breaks the build, and once rather than once per package.

nodes.label: Per-run verdict tables name what is still broken
nodes.norm_label: per-run verdict tables name what is still broken
nodes.rationale: Each run writes a verdict table and the job repeats the list in its step summary, so a red check says which defects are open without anyone opening an artifact or reading the test tree.

nodes.label: Every durable decision is an ADR, written when the decision is taken (D1, D2, D11)
nodes.norm_label: every durable decision is an adr, written when the decision is taken (d1, d2, d11)
nodes.rationale: One file per decision family, NNNN-kebab-case-title.md. Writing it when the work lands leaves long-running decisions unwritten for a whole release and the rejected options already forgotten. Status says what is implemented and what is only decided; Decision is present tense either way, because it is the rule from the moment it is taken.

nodes.label: A changed decision amends its ADR in place (D9)
nodes.norm_label: a changed decision amends its adr in place (d9)
nodes.rationale: Decision states the new rule, Status records the amendment with its date, and the superseded rule is marked superseded rather than deleted, so a reader never finds an old rule stated as current. A reversal amends the ADR; it does not become a new row in a work list.

nodes.label: A ticket is a work list and nothing else (D3, D4)
nodes.norm_label: a ticket is a work list and nothing else (d3, d4)
nodes.rationale: Closed by MOVING the file into the archive subdirectory after everything durable moves out. The extraction is the close; the move is what is left afterwards. An archived file is history and never a source of a current rule - a rule found there is the same process defect as one found in a live ticket.

nodes.norm_label: adr 0019 integration and e2e tests are the product

nodes.norm_label: adr 0022: tickets are work lists that get archived; decisions live in adrs

nodes.norm_label: adr 0031: a test states the target and stays red until the product meets it

nodes.norm_label: adr 0035 the readme advertises, the reference lives under docs/

nodes.norm_label: nothing outside docs/tickets/ may reference a ticket
nodes.rationale: Cite the ADR instead; a comment pointing at a pending change names its ADR, and an archived ticket is as uncitable as a deleted one.

nodes.label: Unit coverage is a floor, not a goal (D13)
nodes.norm_label: unit coverage is a floor, not a goal (d13)
nodes.rationale: A quarter of every uncovered statement was test-double code counted as production code; moving it out raised one package from 13.1% to 81.0% with nothing tested. Any movement from a changed denominator is labelled a denominator correction, not reported as new testing.

nodes.label: The e2e environment runs the documented configuration (D10)
nodes.norm_label: the e2e environment runs the documented configuration (d10)
nodes.rationale: Not the client's insecure defaults - a suite exercising a configuration nobody is told to run is evidence about the wrong system. The bring-up now generates the client's repository password and the preflight fails the whole suite if the repository was created under the published default.

nodes.label: The 2026-09-13 correction: expected-refusal tables are forbidden
nodes.norm_label: the 2026-09-13 correction: expected-refusal tables are forbidden
nodes.rationale: The rclone and s3cmd suites first shipped with every open defect recorded as an EXPECTED refusal, so both suites were green and the release gate reported ready-to-merge while an object written by a single request could be neither uploaded nor fetched back through a documented client. A test states the behaviour the product is supposed to have and is committed red until the product meets it - generalised as ADR 0031.

nodes.label: The suites are part of the product (D1, D2, D14)
nodes.norm_label: the suites are part of the product (d1, d2, d14)
nodes.rationale: Unit tests prove plumbing; they structurally cannot show that stored bytes decrypt, that a real SDK accepts the composed response, or that a backup tool restores what it backed up. Neither suite is disabled, skipped, weakened or deleted to make a change pass, and the moment 'the handler is unit tested' argues for dropping an integration case, the unit suite has done harm.

nodes.label: Every test is shown to fail without the change it covers (D11, D12)
nodes.norm_label: every test is shown to fail without the change it covers (d11, d12)
nodes.rationale: A test that passes against both the fixed and the broken product is not a test. An assertion over fetched output is proven at least once to have read something: an e2e scan of fetched logs passes in silence when the fetch failed or the source was empty, and the suite ran past two data-loss defects that way.

nodes.label: The archive stays out of the knowledge-graph corpus
nodes.norm_label: the archive stays out of the knowledge-graph corpus
nodes.rationale: An archived plan can be read as a current rule, and three things hold that down, none of them a check: D4's extraction duty, D5's reference ban, and keeping the archive out of the corpus so a stale plan is never surfaced as an answer about the product. A reader who opens an archived file directly has no marker in the file telling them its age.

nodes.label: An ADR carries no references into the code (D8)
nodes.norm_label: an adr carries no references into the code (d8)
nodes.rationale: No file paths, line numbers, function, type or package names, no links into the tree: a reader acts on it without opening the repository and it does not go stale when a file is renamed. The product's own vocabulary - configuration keys, s3ep- metadata keys, S3 error codes, header and algorithm names, release versions, shipped commands - is not a code reference and is named exactly.

nodes.label: Nothing outside the ticket directory references a ticket (D5, D6, D7, D10)
nodes.norm_label: nothing outside the ticket directory references a ticket (d5, d6, d7, d10)
nodes.rationale: Work identifiers are not stable - one decision was reversed by a later one in the same series with the only record in a file marked for deletion, and a ticket was renumbered when its release changed. A ticket may reference an ADR; an ADR never references a ticket. A comment pointing at pending work names the ADR by number and title.

nodes.label: ADR numbers are one shared sequence claimed by hand
nodes.norm_label: adr numbers are one shared sequence claimed by hand
nodes.rationale: Two decisions written in parallel can pick the same number and nothing catches it. Enforcement of the whole lifecycle is manual: no CI job looks for a ticket reference in a tracked file or a commit message.

nodes.rationale: In the handler's call into orchestration.Manager; there is no second layer, which is the architectural simplicity goal stated in the main goals.

nodes.label: The internal multipart producer overlaps receive with send
nodes.norm_label: the internal multipart producer overlaps receive with send
nodes.rationale: Bounded pool of concurrency + 1 buffers, and nothing runs after CompleteMultipartUpload: every metadata value exists before the first backend byte, so a finished object is never rewritten (ADR 0024).

nodes.label: A PUT routes on PlaintextContentLength and nothing else
nodes.norm_label: a put routes on plaintextcontentlength and nothing else
nodes.rationale: Above multipart_part_size, or with a length that does not really describe the plaintext, it becomes the internal multipart producer; DecodedContentLength sizes a buffer and decides nothing.

nodes.label: GOMEMLIMIT is not shipped (D15 followed as written)
nodes.norm_label: gomemlimit is not shipped (d15 followed as written)
nodes.rationale: D15 made the value conditional on a measured gain. Under a large-object load the proxy settled at ~98 MiB resident, peaked at 124 MiB from 22 MiB cold against a 512 MiB container limit, so a limit at ~80% is never approached and there is no mechanism for a gain. Accepted with it: the proxy ships on runtime defaults with no out-of-memory guard of its own. GOGC keeps its default while any client-controlled full-body allocation exists.

nodes.label: The local baseline suite (D18, D19, D20, D21)
nodes.norm_label: the local baseline suite (d18, d19, d20, d21)
nodes.rationale: One place, own build tag so no CI workflow picks it up by accident. A run records the machine (processor, cores, memory, kernel, toolchain, container runtime, POWER SOURCE, load average), the commit, tree cleanliness and the stack, writing one machine-readable record and one human summary under a schema version. A ratio is derived at render time and never stored, so a missing leg shows as missing rather than as a plausible ratio; a wide-spread row is marked as carrying no comparison value.

nodes.label: The measurement run cleans up after itself (D13)
nodes.norm_label: the measurement run cleans up after itself (d13)
nodes.rationale: Every bucket it writes to, paged to the end, not behind a switch: a baseline measured against a backend that is fuller on every repetition is not a baseline. Partly met - the pre-run emptying reads one listing page and logs a failure instead of failing, and nothing cleans the two comparison buckets after a run.

nodes.label: The memory bound is a test that fails, not a number in a report (D14)
nodes.norm_label: the memory bound is a test that fails, not a number in a report (d14)
nodes.rationale: The one performance-adjacent assertion allowed to fail a build, carved out of D11: how much memory a process holds under a defined load is a property of the CODE, it does not drift with runner load, so exceeding it is a defect rather than a slow day. It samples process_resident_memory_bytes and asserts peak-minus-idle against a bound derived from multipart_part_size, multipart_upload_concurrency and multipart_short_part_buffer_size. It runs in the local suite only, which is a real gap.

nodes.label: A performance number is a proxy/direct ratio, never an absolute (D6, D12, D16)
nodes.norm_label: a performance number is a proxy/direct ratio, never an absolute (d6, d12, d16)
nodes.rationale: A new benchmark of a request path is born with a direct-to-backend leg measured in the same run, or it is a profiling harness and is named as one - a single-leg number cannot separate a slower proxy from a slower machine. Absolutes are still published, described as a proxy path against a direct path, and never labelled 'the cost of encryption'.

nodes.label: A recorded run, not a threshold, is the unit of comparison (D8, D9, D10)
nodes.norm_label: a recorded run, not a threshold, is the unit of comparison (d8, d9, d10)
nodes.rationale: There is no threshold table any more. A baseline is re-taken whenever a change is expected to move throughput, and the newer run becomes what the next change is judged against: keeping an old run after a known gain hides tomorrow's loss inside yesterday's slack. A ratio worse than roughly a third of the direct path is reported as a finding rather than encoded.

nodes.label: In-flight memory is bounded and configured (D4)
nodes.norm_label: in-flight memory is bounded and configured (d4)
nodes.rationale: multipart_upload_concurrency + 1 buffers of multipart_part_size each - one per upload worker plus the one being filled - and that is what an operator budgets against the container limit. Overlapping transfers may not raise the bound. Its interaction with the short-part buffer bound of ADR 0011 has not been worked through; both hold parts in memory.

nodes.label: An upload forwards bytes while still receiving them (D1)
nodes.norm_label: an upload forwards bytes while still receiving them (d1)
nodes.rationale: Three places still fill a buffer first: the internal producer (which cuts parts itself but overlaps encryption and the next part), the pass-through provider's UploadPart, and a client part an encrypting provider cannot forward - short, misaligned, or with a length the request does not declare - because it may have to be sealed at Complete.

nodes.label: optimizations.max_request_document_size (D8)
nodes.rationale: One ceiling over every request document the proxy buffers whole - the bodies D4 never counted, because they are not parts. Default set so the proxy refuses nothing S3 itself accepts: the largest legal document is a Delete naming a thousand 1024-byte keys, about 1.1 MB. Above it, 400 EntityTooLarge before the backend is called, counting what ARRIVES rather than what Content-Length declares. A written 0 refuses the start. It is a memory bound and nothing else - a Delete naming more than a thousand objects is 400 MalformedXML whatever its size.

nodes.label: Receiving overlaps sending, and sealing never serialises the pipeline (D2, D3)
nodes.norm_label: receiving overlaps sending, and sealing never serialises the pipeline (d2, d3)
nodes.rationale: The producer never blocks on an upload it has already dispatched, and because segments are independent, parts are encrypted concurrently with the transfers of other parts.

nodes.label: A part stays retriable from a retained copy (D5)
nodes.norm_label: a part stays retriable from a retained copy (d5)
nodes.rationale: The proxy never asks the client for the same bytes twice, so overlap buys latency and not memory. A decision, not a design: the retry was never built, the AWS SDK does not replay a body it cannot rewind, and since 2026-09-12 it can only ever cover the internal producer - a streamed client part has no retained copy, and the client re-sends it, which S3 semantics already allow.

nodes.norm_label: no switch, flag or configuration value disarms an assertion (d4)
nodes.rationale: The only legitimate skip is a suite skipping itself when the backend or proxy it needs is unreachable; build tags select which suite runs, never soften one. A disarm switch gets set the first time the gate is inconvenient and never unset - which is exactly what happened to the performance thresholds.

nodes.label: A performance change carries a before and an after (D1, D4, D5)
nodes.norm_label: a performance change carries a before and an after (d1, d4, d5)
nodes.rationale: Fresh stack, at least three runs, median, against a baseline on the same machine at the pre-change commit. A regression stops work rather than shipping with an explanation. A defect on a path a scheduled rewrite replaces is deferred only WITH the obligation recorded: the number to beat and the instrument that will measure it, built if it does not exist.

nodes.label: Both candidate paths are measured and the loser is deleted (D2)
nodes.norm_label: both candidate paths are measured and the loser is deleted (d2)
nodes.rationale: A performance choice is never left configurable, and never left reachable by accident of middleware composition - a choice that depends on the deployment is a choice nobody made. The motivating defect was a pooled copy buffer believed to be switched by an unrelated monitoring flag; a second unconditional wrapper meant the flag never mattered.

nodes.label: No throughput measurement fails a build (D11)
nodes.norm_label: no throughput measurement fails a build (d11)
nodes.rationale: Removing the assertion is what removed the switch that disarmed it - there is nothing left for a switch to hide. A throughput number is a property of the machine that produced it, so asserting on one teaches people to ignore red. A 100 MB case failed at 17.6% inside the full suite and passed when run alone.

nodes.label: Nothing mechanical stops a regression from being merged
nodes.norm_label: nothing mechanical stops a regression from being merged
nodes.rationale: The central accepted risk and the price of the 2026-09-09 amendment: the obligation rests on the person making the change running the local suite on both commits, written into the success criteria of changes that need it. The ratio is also blind to a uniform slowdown - if the backend or machine regresses, both legs move together.

nodes.label: CI measures once, publishes, and moves on (D7, D22)
nodes.norm_label: ci measures once, publishes, and moves on (d7, d22)
nodes.rationale: Repetitions belong to the local suite: repetitions across nine sizes on two transports move tens of gibibytes and take minutes, and the pipeline is already long. When a more trustworthy number conflicts with a slower pipeline, the number is taken locally.

nodes.label: The unconsumed ranged-read body that killed connection pooling
nodes.norm_label: the unconsumed ranged-read body that killed connection pooling
nodes.rationale: A ranged read fetched a provisional window and consumed only the real one, so the backend body was closed with bytes unread and Go's transport dropped the connection instead of pooling it: a 1 MiB ranged read ran at 155 MiB/s against a backend doing 220. It is the path kopia reads on, had been in the release since the segment chain landed, and no gate would have caught it - every functional suite passed throughout.

nodes.label: The multipart deficit is per byte, not per request
nodes.norm_label: the multipart deficit is per byte, not per request
nodes.rationale: Everything else was measured and ruled out: the post-completion rewrite runs at 4826-7485 MiB/s (a twentieth of the gap, not the whole of it), the extra hop is paid by the faster streaming path too, the cipher is 3.8-6.1% of per-byte upload time, the old integrity pass 7.7%. A size sweep from 8 to 256 MiB settles at ~1.45x from six parts upward, so the cost is the serialisation itself: no byte of a part moves until the last byte of that part has arrived and been encrypted.

nodes.label: The restructuring ships with the format change, not after it (D6, D7)
nodes.norm_label: the restructuring ships with the format change, not after it (d6, d7)
nodes.rationale: A path rewritten once is measured once; deferring to 5.1 means writing and measuring it twice. No upload speed-up may be claimed until the three-leg comparison is re-run and has moved - and even then the gain cannot be attributed to this decision alone, because the format change, the producer restructuring and the self-copy removal landed in one commit.

nodes.rationale: Never by round-tripping through the proxy: a proxy that decrypts its own output proves nothing about what was stored. All three e2e suites now share one assertion function, each passing its own backend client and its own spelling of the stored contract; the migration immediately paid for itself because the shared assertion checks all four metadata keys and the Velero copy had been checking three.

nodes.label: existingSecret is a first-class arm (D4)
nodes.rationale: A Secret holding tls.crt and tls.key is mounted and nothing is issued, so cert-manager is not required at all - which matters for clusters that do not run it and for a certificate minted by something else. On this arm the operator owns the names; the chart does not check them against the Service it renders, which is why the e2e certificate lists the four names by hand.

nodes.label: The chart-issued certificate covers the four Service names it computes (D2)
nodes.norm_label: the chart-issued certificate covers the four service names it computes (d2)
nodes.rationale: <fullname>, .<namespace>, .svc and .svc.<clusterDomain>, from the release and namespace rather than names an operator keeps in sync. An operator may add more but may not replace these: a name the Service answers to and the certificate does not is a failure the operator only sees when a client refuses the connection. A wildcard was rejected - it would cover every service in the namespace.

nodes.label: clusterDomain (cluster.local) must be set by hand
nodes.norm_label: clusterdomain (cluster.local) must be set by hand
nodes.rationale: Helm cannot discover it - a lookup would need a live cluster and would make helm template behave differently from helm install - and guessing would produce a certificate that fails verification for the one name most clients use.

nodes.label: The Ingress is not replaced and not deprecated (D8)
nodes.norm_label: the ingress is not replaced and not deprecated (d8)
nodes.rationale: The two are independent: a deployment may do both, and one that does neither is refused only if it CLAIMS to do one.

nodes.label: The probe scheme is derived from both TLS sources (D6)
nodes.norm_label: the probe scheme is derived from both tls sources (d6)
nodes.rationale: tls.enabled inside the operator's config OR serviceTLS.enabled. A derivation that looked only at the first would probe a TLS listener in plaintext and the pod would never become Ready - the original defect this project already fixed once, reintroduced through the new door. A second values key for the scheme was rejected: two sources of truth drift, and the one that loses is the one nobody looks at.

A workaround in the tree that long is not a workaround, it is the missing feature being paid for over and over.

nodes.rationale: No mapping index anywhere the backend can reach: a stored mapping object makes every lookup depend on something a hostile backend can withhold, serve selectively or roll back - a denial of service and a rollback oracle in one object. Randomised encryption is unusable because an exact GET cannot recompute the stored key a prior write produced. The cost is that deterministic means dictionary-attackable.

nodes.norm_label: no fingerprint is special-cased on the read path (d6, d7)
nodes.rationale: The old pass-through unwrap was taken whenever OBJECT METADATA named its fingerprint, whatever the configured provider was - a forgery oracle: choose a data key, store it verbatim, seal any plaintext under it, and every segment authenticates. The exit provider holds no key material and both of its key operations return an error, so a backend labelling an object with the exit fingerprint gets a refusal rather than a data key of its own choosing.

nodes.label: One proxy beside each S3 client, inside the cluster

That traffic carries SigV4 credentials, every object key in a URL and the plaintext of every object, so a proxy that decrypts and hands it over a plaintext Service has moved the exposure rather than removed it.

A merge has to decide which side wins per key, that decision is invisible in the values file, and the failure it produces is a proxy serving with a certificate the operator did not think they configured.
