They must never be confused. Routine rotation is only free because the key version is not part of the fingerprint - that is the design constraint everything hangs on.

nodes.label: Vault Transit As A KEK Provider
nodes.norm_label: vault transit as a kek provider
nodes.rationale: Talk to the Transit engine directly with a widely used library rather than completing the Tink stub, which would have existed solely as a wrapper around one HTTP call on a deprecated module path.

nodes.label: The HMAC Is The Entire Difference
nodes.norm_label: the hmac is the entire difference
nodes.rationale: HMAC-SHA256 runs at 3092 MiB/s against AES-CTR at 10475, so the large-object path can never exceed the HMAC however fast the cipher is. In the proxy's own profile SHA-256 is 17.30 percent flat against AES-CTR 5.17 - the integrity pass is 3.3x the cipher it protects.

nodes.label: The Container Memory Limit Is Nowhere Near Reached
nodes.norm_label: the container memory limit is nowhere near reached
nodes.rationale: Settled idle 97.7 MiB, peak under load 124.1, container limit 512. A GOMEMLIMIT at about 400 MiB is never approached, so the collector has no reason to behave differently and there is no mechanism for a 3-5 percent gain; the honest outcome may be to ship it as an out-of-memory guard and claim no throughput benefit.

nodes.label: Ranged Reads: The Alignment Before-Column
nodes.rationale: A deliberately unaligned offset is indistinguishable from an aligned one at 1 MiB and above because AES-CTR seeks to any byte. A segment chain cannot, so these numbers are the only before-column for the row to watch after the format change - measured before the code that will make them interesting existed.

nodes.label: The Proxy Barely Gets Faster With More Clients
nodes.norm_label: the proxy barely gets faster with more clients
nodes.rationale: The backend scales 2.8x from one client to eight while the proxy gains 1.3x and gives it back at 32. Identical on both transports, so not a transport effect; at 64 KiB the proxy runs far below the crypto floor, so not bandwidth. Where the serialisation lives is not established - the CPU profile was taken under large-object load.

nodes.label: RSA Unwrap Is Four Orders Of Magnitude Off The Local Provider
nodes.norm_label: rsa unwrap is four orders of magnitude off the local provider
nodes.rationale: AES-256 unwrap 146 ns against RSA-4096 3.80 ms - 26000x. The wrap column is far closer because wrapping uses the public exponent; it is the read path that pays. This is the measurement behind keeping one local key provider.

nodes.label: Upload Falls Off A Cliff At The Routing Threshold
nodes.norm_label: upload falls off a cliff at the routing threshold
nodes.rationale: At and above 5 MiB the ratio drops from 72.2 to 59.3 percent and stays near 56-60, while every download row sits at 96.5 to 110.7 percent of direct. The crypto headroom is nearly worthless end to end - crypto is 3.8 to 6.1 percent of per-byte time - so the cliff points at the second write instead. Stated explicitly as a hypothesis: the self-copy was not timed in isolation.

nodes.label: The Self-Copy Is Not The Cause
nodes.norm_label: the self-copy is not the cause
nodes.rationale: The model needed the self-copy to run at 231-372 MiB/s; timed directly it runs at 4826-7485, an order of magnitude faster, costing about 5 percent of the gap. The hypothesis fitted three points and was wrong, which is what a model that has never been checked against the thing it models is worth.

nodes.label: The Proxy Is Faster Than The Backend When It Streams
nodes.norm_label: the proxy is faster than the backend when it streams
nodes.rationale: The streaming leg is at or above the direct backend while encrypting every byte and crossing loopback twice, so neither the cipher, nor the checksum, nor the second write, nor the extra hop is what the ratio pays for. 87 percent of the gap is the auto-multipart write path itself. Which of its two structural differences carries it is not established - attribute before fixing.

nodes.label: The Deficit Is Per Byte, Not Per Request
nodes.norm_label: the deficit is per byte, not per request
nodes.rationale: At 256 MiB the four backend calls amortise into nothing and the integrity pass is about 14 percent; three quarters of the gap scales with the bytes, and the only per-byte difference is that one leg forwards while it reads. The factor is worst at one part (1.96x) and settles near 1.45x from six parts up - the signature of a serialisation inside one part, not between parts.

nodes.label: pre-v2 Baseline Findings
nodes.rationale: The before column for the storage format change. Written the day the numbers were taken, stating what they support, what they only suggest, and what they cannot answer; derived and single-sample figures are marked as such.

nodes.label: The Segment Codec, Measured
nodes.rationale: The prediction was 3.4x from a model of raw cipher calls; the shipped codec measures 1.74-1.87x. The gap is the CRC32C the model did not run, plus segment framing and the trailer. The model rows stay in the suite as a ceiling, not a target: the checksum is decided.

nodes.label: Upload Path Decomposition
nodes.rationale: Decomposes the upload deficit, falsifies the explanation the pre-v2 findings proposed and identifies the real one. Taken on battery, so its figures are comparable only within the run.

nodes.label: The Before-Column For The Producer Restructuring
nodes.norm_label: the before-column for the producer restructuring
nodes.rationale: A decision like ADR 0024's is worth nothing without the column it will be judged against. On mains, clean tree, all twelve upload rows stable at 1.0-6.3 percent RSD, which is what makes the factors readable. The direct leg is dropped above 16 MiB because the backend refuses an aws-chunked chunk above that size.

nodes.label: The DEK Cache Lifetime Becomes A Security Parameter
nodes.norm_label: the dek cache lifetime becomes a security parameter
nodes.rationale: With a network-backed provider the cache stops being an optimisation: it keeps repeat reads off the network, and a cached key keeps serving after Vault access is revoked. No value is right for both concerns. Today it is an LRU bounded at 1024 with no expiry at all; adding one is a prerequisite, not part of the work. There is also no request coalescing around the unwrap, so parallel ranged reads would burst identical Vault calls.

nodes.label: Key Custody Is What This Buys, And Only That
nodes.norm_label: key custody is what this buys, and only that
nodes.rationale: The key leaves the configuration file and the deployment secret. A compromised proxy still holds plaintext and can still ask Vault to unwrap anything it can present, for as long as its token is valid. Any sentence that blurs the two is a claim the product does not honour.

nodes.label: A Rewrap Campaign Is Not A Metadata Edit
nodes.norm_label: a rewrap campaign is not a metadata edit
nodes.rationale: Writing a rewrapped key back means a server-side copy that replaces metadata, and S3 rewrites the object to do that: a 5 TB campaign is a 5 TB rewrite even though no ciphertext byte changes. On a versioned or object-locked bucket it cannot retire a key version at all. It cannot run through the proxy - a copy primitive there would be a metadata-rewrite primitive for every authenticated client.

nodes.label: Vault Availability Becomes Proxy Availability
nodes.rationale: Cold reads fail during an outage and the proxy refuses to start without a reachable key, which during a rolling update turns an outage into a deployment that cannot scale back up. Correct and dangerous; it belongs in the operator documentation as the headline.

nodes.label: Verify First: Nothing Here Was Checkable
nodes.norm_label: verify first: nothing here was checkable
nodes.rationale: The design was written without network access, so every statement about the Vault API is from knowledge; the first task is an afternoon of curl against the demo Vault, capturing real request and response bodies into the file.

nodes.label: The GCM Profile Rows Are TLS Records, Not Object Crypto
nodes.norm_label: the gcm profile rows are tls records, not object crypto
nodes.rationale: pprof -peek reaches gcmAesEnc/Dec only through crypto/tls xorNonceAEAD: they are the proxy-to-backend hop. Counting them as object crypto is exactly the misattribution this project has already made once and that the measurement rules were written to prevent.

nodes.label: Two Measurement Bugs Found Before The Run
nodes.norm_label: two measurement bugs found before the run
nodes.rationale: One variant allocated a destination per repetition while the other reused one, and the segmented decrypt allocated per segment - two thousand allocations for a 128 MiB object. A comparison between two crypto paths is only valid if both allocate the same amount, which for a throughput number means both allocating nothing.

nodes.label: A 1.7x That Was Nearly A 1.0x
nodes.rationale: Two implementation choices cost the entire gain: folding the CRC per 64 KiB segment with the GF(2) matrix construction (4523 against 12107 MB/s for a running checksum - the fold belongs at part granularity), and copying every byte into the writer's pending buffer even when the caller handed over a whole segment. The lesson: an instrument comparing a model against a real path measures the model.

nodes.label: Same Machine, Same Power Source
nodes.rationale: The battery run of the same morning reproduces the shared sizes within noise - the battery made both legs slower together rather than distorting the comparison - but the mains run is the before-column because the run that follows it will be on mains too.

nodes.label: The Ranged-Read Window and Its Amplification Bound
nodes.norm_label: the ranged-read window and its amplification bound

nodes.label: Which Range Headers Are Acted On Is Decided Twice
nodes.norm_label: which range headers are acted on is decided twice

nodes.label: 5.0.0: an unknown configuration key stops the start
nodes.norm_label: 5.0.0: an unknown configuration key stops the start
nodes.rationale: Removed keys and misspelled ones both refuse; the configured clock skew now applies to header authentication, pre-signed URLs default to one hour rather than seven days, and a backend endpoint must carry a scheme and be https under an encrypting provider.

nodes.label: An authentication refusal answers the code that names what failed (D13)
nodes.norm_label: an authentication refusal answers the code that names what failed (d13)
nodes.rationale: 400 means the request itself is unusable, 403 that it was understood and refused. Anonymous is 403 AccessDenied, an unimplemented scheme 400 InvalidRequest, an unparseable header 400 AuthorizationHeaderMalformed, then 403 InvalidAccessKeyId, 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch and 403 RequestTimeTooSkewed. Where MinIO and AWS disagree the proxy follows AWS, because clients branch on the code.

nodes.label: s3_security.max_clock_skew_seconds
nodes.rationale: Default 900, governs both authentication forms after previously applying only to the pre-signed path; a configured 0 is refused at startup because the value an operator picks to mean 'no tolerance' used to widen the window to the default maximum.

nodes.label: s3_security.max_presign_expiry_seconds
nodes.rationale: Default 3600s with a hard cap of 604800s (the S3 seven-day maximum). Seven days of bearer capability is the wrong default for a proxy whose purpose is to bound exposure; the cap stays at the S3 maximum so a configured value cannot put the proxy outside what an S3 client expects.

nodes.label: Profiling endpoints on a loopback-only listener
nodes.norm_label: profiling endpoints on a loopback-only listener
nodes.rationale: A non-loopback address for them is a startup error, because a heap profile of this process contains key material and plaintext. The monitoring listener carries no authentication and is fenced by the network.

nodes.label: s3_clients static credentials (D2)
nodes.rationale: At least one entry required or startup fails; access_key_id at least 8 chars, secret_key at least 16, duplicate key ids a startup error - a secret of that minimum length is not guessable, which is why brute-force defence at this door is a fiction.

nodes.label: SigV4 in both forms (D1)
nodes.rationale: Real S3 clients use header signing on the data path and pre-signed URLs for retrieval; supporting only one form breaks a backup tool that does both, so neither is a degraded mode.

nodes.label: A token without an exp claim is invalid (D3)
nodes.norm_label: a token without an exp claim is invalid (d3)
nodes.rationale: Validation checked expiry only when present, so a token with no exp was accepted, the stored expiry kept its zero value (year one), and the hourly check killed the process after 60 minutes blaming an expiry that did not exist - a permanent hourly crash loop pointing at the wrong cause. A perpetual license must be an explicit claim, never an omission.

nodes.label: An invalid configuration VALUE refuses the start and the error names the field (D8)
nodes.norm_label: an invalid configuration value refuses the start and the error names the field (d8)
nodes.rationale: Silent fixups are not offered. This is why the same release refuses an optimizations.multipart_part_size that is not a multiple of 65536 and an encryption.providers[].config.aes_key that is not base64 of exactly 32 acceptable bytes, rather than starting and failing the first upload larger than one part.

nodes.label: Render-time refusals instead of crashloops (D5, D9, D10)
nodes.norm_label: render-time refusals instead of crashloops (d5, d9, d10)
nodes.rationale: serviceTLS.enabled with neither existingSecret nor an issuer refuses the render and names both values, because otherwise the pod starts, fails to read its certificate and crashloops with the reason in a log nobody watches. An enabled Ingress must terminate TLS for EVERY host it serves - covering the rule set is the bar, not a non-empty tls block, because the hop that stays plaintext is the one nobody listed. A cert-manager Certificate must have a consumer the chart can see, because it is the one part of a TLS setup that reports itself healthy while nothing uses it.

nodes.label: SigV4 client authentication
nodes.rationale: No S3 path is anonymous because the proxy holds the backend credential itself; only the two probe endpoints are unsigned and they answer nothing about the data.

nodes.label: One clock-skew window governs both authentication forms
nodes.norm_label: one clock-skew window governs both authentication forms
nodes.rationale: The header form used to compare against a compile-time constant, so narrowing the window narrowed only the pre-signed path. 0 is refused rather than read as the default; the window is a replay window and the proxy keeps no nonce cache.

nodes.label: An http:// backend endpoint refuses the start
nodes.norm_label: an http:// backend endpoint refuses the start
nodes.rationale: The backend credential would travel in a SigV4 header over plaintext and a listener learns every key name and object size; under exit the reason is stronger, because the object bytes travel in the clear too.

nodes.label: No multi-tenancy, no per-client keys or scopes
nodes.norm_label: no multi-tenancy, no per-client keys or scopes
nodes.rationale: Every authenticated client can do everything any other can, and all write under the same global KEK; if tenant separation is needed, run one proxy per tenant with its own KEK and credentials.

nodes.label: One broad backend credential, 52 interface methods all called
nodes.norm_label: one broad backend credential, 52 interface methods all called
nodes.rationale: A declared method is a capability the credential is expected to have, so an interface naming operations no code issues overstates the privilege the deployment needs; the realistic hardening is scoping the credential to the one bucket.

nodes.label: Two authentication forms: header and pre-signed query
nodes.norm_label: two authentication forms: header and pre-signed query
nodes.rationale: Both are needed by real clients: Velero signs headers on its data path and uses pre-signed URLs for backup and restore log downloads.

nodes.label: ADR 0014 Authentication is SigV4, no rate limiting
nodes.norm_label: adr 0014 authentication is sigv4, no rate limiting

nodes.label: ADR 0012 D15: The SigV4 payload hash is verified when s3_security.verify_payload_hash is on
nodes.norm_label: adr 0012 d15: the sigv4 payload hash is verified when s3_security.verify_payload_hash is on

nodes.label: Canonical query string sorts by parameter name, not by name=value
nodes.norm_label: canonical query string sorts by parameter name, not by name=value
nodes.rationale: The two orders agree until one name prefixes another: ?select=&select-type=2 was signed as select-type=2&select=, so every SelectObjectContent answered 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch. It failed closed - a wrong canonical request can only refuse a good signature - which is why it survived.

nodes.label: Per-chunk aws-chunked signatures are not verified (D6)
nodes.norm_label: per-chunk aws-chunked signatures are not verified (d6)
nodes.rationale: The seed signature in the Authorization header is verified; chunk signatures protect the operator-controlled client leg, which is not the adversary. TLS is the mitigation there, and it is also what makes an AWS SDK pick the unsigned-trailer framing.

nodes.label: The client address is a log field, never an identity (D8)
nodes.norm_label: the client address is a log field, never an identity (d8)
nodes.rationale: remote_addr and x_forwarded_for are logged raw and interpreted by nothing, so there is no trusted-proxy list to configure. The removed per-address failure map was keyed on a caller-chosen header, unbounded, and written unsynchronised - concurrent map writes terminate a Go process, so two bad-signature requests were a remote kill switch.

nodes.label: A control that exists only in configuration or documentation is worse than none
nodes.norm_label: a control that exists only in configuration or documentation is worse than none
nodes.rationale: The recurring principle of this ADR family: a dead s3_security key, an assertion-disarming switch, a warning nobody is forced to read, a safe shape written as a comment beside an unsafe literal, and a chart rule that lives only in the values file are all the same defect - a control that gets relied upon because it looks like one.

nodes.label: A key that reads nothing is removed, not documented (D9, D12)
nodes.norm_label: a key that reads nothing is removed, not documented (d9, d12)
nodes.rationale: enable_rate_limiting, max_requests_per_minute, max_failed_attempts, unblock_ip_seconds, strict_signature_validation and enable_security_logging were parsed, validated, documented and read by nothing. A control that exists only in configuration is worse than no control because it gets relied upon. Throttling, if ever wanted, arrives with the code that reads it and a test that proves it throttles.

nodes.label: Replay inside the signature validity window is undefended
nodes.norm_label: replay inside the signature validity window is undefended
nodes.rationale: There is no nonce store, so a captured signed request or a leaked pre-signed URL replays until its timestamp ages out. The clock-skew window is a freshness bound, not a replay defence. Whether a nonce store is ever built is open.

nodes.label: No document, example or default ever prints a usable key (D8)
nodes.norm_label: no document, example or default ever prints a usable key (d8)
nodes.rationale: A safe shape written as a comment beside an unsafe literal is documentation, not a control. Example configurations are live fixtures - the demo stack mounts two as running proxies' configuration - so one key in three of them puts the same repository-public key on three deployments.

nodes.label: The canonical request is built the way the signer builds it
nodes.norm_label: the canonical request is built the way the signer builds it
nodes.rationale: Trimming only, without collapsing interior space runs, answered SignatureDoesNotMatch to correctly signed requests the backend accepted - Content-Disposition filenames in pre-signed download URLs were where it showed. The failure was always a false negative, never a false positive.

nodes.norm_label: the proxy owns the part layout

nodes.label: Unauthenticated probe paths /livez and /readyz (D11, D14)
nodes.rationale: Served ahead of the authentication middleware. A request is the probe only when unsigned and carrying no query string; anything else to those paths is an S3 request for a bucket of that name. Reserving the names would make two legal bucket names unreachable without saying so anywhere - the probe keeps its exemption, the name does not.

nodes.label: terminationGracePeriodSeconds derived from shutdown_timeout (D5)
nodes.rationale: Derived rather than configured apart so the platform cannot kill the process before its own budget expires. Amended 2026-09-15 (ADR 0034 D11) to the sum of the preStop hold, shutdown_timeout and five seconds; an explicit override below that sum now fails the render instead of winning silently.

nodes.label: read_header_timeout (30s) and idle_timeout (60s), never 0
nodes.rationale: These bound what is NOT a transfer. With every budget at zero, a connection that never completes its headers (the classic slow-header attack) and a keep-alive connection that never sends another request would both be held forever, so startup refuses 0.

nodes.label: read_timeout / write_timeout (default 0 = no deadline)
nodes.rationale: The rejected alternative attacked a finite default, not the key itself; at 0 the shipped behaviour is D1 for anyone who configures nothing, and the key is an escape hatch for a deployment that knows its own numbers.

nodes.label: shutdown_timeout as the single shutdown budget (D4)
nodes.norm_label: shutdown_timeout as the single shutdown budget (d4)
nodes.rationale: 30s when unset or zero. Since ADR 0029 it covers the whole shutdown: the drain, the multipart sweep and the listener close each get what is left of the one budget, so all three stay inside the platform grace period derived from it. It is now the only server-side limit on a running transfer.

nodes.norm_label: no rate limiting and no per-address blocking (d7)
nodes.rationale: Per-address blocking is the wrong instrument: one legitimate client is one authenticated identity bursting from one address, and anything behind NAT or an ingress looks the same. Denial-of-service defence belongs in the ingress, which can actually do it. The proxy also ships no configuration key that suggests otherwise.

nodes.label: The backend's own ~25s stall tolerance sets a ~2.6 KiB/s floor

nodes.rationale: The proxy opens the backend request and sends nothing until it has a whole segment to seal, so a slow client turns into a silent backend request; MinIO answers 503 with a resource-lock timeout after roughly 25 seconds. D1's promise is therefore not 'any speed'. Closing the gap is an undecided design question.

nodes.label: Bounding an unproductive connection is the ingress's job (D6)
nodes.norm_label: bounding an unproductive connection is the ingress's job (d6)
nodes.rationale: The proxy ships no rate limit, no connection cap and no per-transfer progress deadline; a client sending one byte per minute holds a goroutine indefinitely and the mitigation is external. Per-connection progress deadlines were kept as an option to revisit, not built.

nodes.label: No wall-clock budget on a body transfer (D1)
nodes.norm_label: no wall-clock budget on a body transfer (d1)
nodes.rationale: Two fixed 30-second budgets made the maximum servable object a function of client bandwidth (~3.6 GB at 1 Gbit/s), resetting healthy transfers mid-stream with no actionable error. The bug survived every benchmark because the suites run on loopback with parts that finish in under a second.

nodes.label: A response wrapper preserves flush, hijack and the underlying writer (D9)
nodes.norm_label: a response wrapper preserves flush, hijack and the underlying writer (d9)
